Strict session IDs for raw PHP apps#

This page covers session-strict-mode: which apps it is for, the line it adds, what counts as already covered, and what makes it refuse. Before this: Hand-copied libraries to Composer. Next: Laravel hops and vendor/.

PHP ships with session.use_strict_mode off. With it off, PHP takes any session ID a browser sends, even one the server never handed out, and starts a session under it. That is the door session fixation walks through: someone plants an ID on a victim, waits for the victim to sign in, and then rides the same session. With strict mode on, PHP throws an unknown ID away and issues a fresh one. session.use_only_cookies (on by default) keeps the ID out of URLs.

HELMET sets both for apps that boot it, and Laravel runs its own session store, so neither needs this hop. It is for the older raw PHP apps that call plain session_start() and use none of the stack's packages.

In two commands#

booster plan --path=<app> --strict-session            # the calls it would cover, or the stop signs that block it
booster run --path=<app> --strict-session --dry-run   # read the diff, then run again without --dry-run

Without --strict-session the plan still finds the calls and says so:

The app starts PHP sessions without strict session IDs (3 session_start() calls in 2 files). Add --strict-session to plan the hop that turns them on.

--only session-strict-mode (with --strict-session) runs just this hop. The planner puts it first, on the PHP the app runs today, so its gate proves this one change, and the hardening lands even when a later hop stalls.

The line it adds#

Before the statement that holds each session_start() call, Booster adds one comment and one guarded line, at the same indent:

// Booster: strict session IDs, set before the session starts (refuses IDs this server never issued).
if (session_status() === PHP_SESSION_NONE && !headers_sent()) { ini_set('session.use_strict_mode', '1'); ini_set('session.use_only_cookies', '1'); }
session_start();

The guard matters. PHP warns when a session setting changes while a session is active or after output has gone out, and in both cases session_start() would not start a new session anyway, so the line simply steps aside. The hop never adds a warning to a page.

"Before the statement" means the whole statement: a braceless if (...) session_start(); gets the line above the if, an else session_start(); gets it above the if it belongs to, and a call inside a match arm gets it above the match. A call that shares its line with other code (minified files, <?php session_start(); ?> in a template) gets the guard inline, right before it. Booster reads the file with PHP's own tokenizer, skips comments, strings and methods named session_start, and checks that every file it edits still parses.

Why a line in the code, not a config file#

  • Not .user.ini. PHP reads .user.ini files only under CGI and FastCGI. Citadel runs PHP as an Apache module, which never reads one, so a .user.ini would look like a fix and do nothing.
  • Not .htaccess. php_flag lines work under the Apache module but are a server error under PHP-FPM, and Booster's changes must keep working off Citadel too.
  • Not HELMET. helmet_boot() sets both options and much more, but it also renames the session cookie, which signs everyone out once, and it adds headers. That is a bigger change than this hop promises, so an app that requires HELMET gets a MANUAL line suggesting it instead.

A php.ini change on Citadel would cover every app at once. That is a separate proposal, not this hop.

Already covered, left alone#

The hop changes nothing for:

  • a Laravel app (the planner skips it and says why),
  • an app that calls helmet_boot() or SessionHardening::apply(),
  • an app whose root .htaccess or .squire/php.ini sets session.use_strict_mode,
  • files under a folder whose own .htaccess sets it,
  • a file that already names session.use_strict_mode (including the line this hop wrote),
  • vendor/ and node_modules/.

So a second run changes nothing. Any other php.ini in the repository (a Docker one, say) is noted, but Citadel's PHP does not read it, so the hop still adds the lines.

Stop signs#

Strict mode changes how some apps hand out session IDs. When Booster finds one of these, it refuses, changes nothing, and names each one:

Stop sign Why
session_id($id) with an argument The app sets the ID itself; strict mode would replace an ID the server never issued
The SID constant It carries the session ID in URLs, which cookie-only IDs drop
session.use_trans_sid on Session IDs travel in URLs
session.use_only_cookies or session.use_cookies off The app expects IDs to arrive some other way
<?= session_start() ?> No statement can go inside an echo tag

These are read from ini_set() calls, session_start([...]) options, .htaccess and ini files. A value Booster cannot read (a variable, say) counts as a stop sign. Settings that keep IDs in cookies, such as ini_set('session.use_trans_sid', false), are fine. After fixing or reviewing each one, set the two options by hand where it is safe.

By hand, after the run#

  • Sign in on pre-production. Sign in, use a page that keeps session data, and sign out. A session the server already holds keeps working; a browser that sends an ID the server never issued gets a fresh one.
  • Custom session handlers. An app that calls session_set_save_handler() only gets strict mode when its handler implements validateId() (SessionUpdateTimestampHandlerInterface). PHP's own SessionHandler class does not. The hop names each handler as a MANUAL line.

Official notes: session.use_strict_mode and session management basics.
